title: Row-reduced column generation for degenerate master problems
contribution: Methodological paper without computation that generalizes the improved primal simplex and dynamic constraints aggregation to row-reduced column generation: with a degenerate restricted master it keeps only the rows of positive variables, prices compatible columns (cSP) or convex combinations of incompatible ones (rSP, itself solved by column generation), and obtains from rSP a necessary and sufficient LP optimality condition.
problem_entry: Tailing-off of column generation, blamed on degenerate restricted master solutions, above all in LP relaxations of combinatorial problems (p. 2); entered by carrying recent anti-degeneracy advances of the primal simplex (IPS) into column generation, in a self-declared methodological paper (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Keep only the p rows of positive basic variables (RrRMP with a p x p working basis, pp. 4-5); price compatible columns, whose transformed part on the dropped rows is zero, by cSP (the pricing problem plus linear compatibility constraints), otherwise a convex combination of incompatible columns by rSP, itself solved by column generation (pp. 6-7); algorithm RrCG (p. 9).
assumptions: LP master in standard form with m artificials, A of full row rank (p. 3); columns encode combinatorial objects whose cost is typically non-linear (p. 3); linearly independent positive columns, no restriction for simplex solutions (p. 4); inequalities via surplus variables (pp. 7-8); interpretations for set partitioning and minimum cost flow (p. 11); no instances.
proof_devices: Theorem 1: necessary and sufficient LP optimality condition from rSP, proved by a dual-feasible construction and an improving convex combination (p. 10)
Proposition 1: a column is compatible iff it lies in the span of A_F (pp. 10-11)
Propositions 2-3: cSP and rSP independent of the working basis, by row duplication and left-multiplication (appendix, pp. 15-17)
Row subset Q of P as a partial pricing strategy; leaving the row partition unchanged after a pivot still gives an exact algorithm (p. 13)
experiments: none; the computational promise is credited to the cited IPS and DCA experiments (pp. 1-2, 14)
positioning: Generalizes IPS (Elhallaoui et al. 2010a; Raymond et al. 2010) and DCA (Elhallaoui et al. 2005, 2008, 2010b), likens row reduction to Pan's deficient basis (p. 2), and treats IPS as a special case of RrCG (p. 9).
writing: Self-declared methodological paper with hedged claims ('may take advantage', p. 1); a result stated as a theorem because it was 'not explicitly stated in previous IPS papers' (p. 10); short proofs and one interpretation section (p. 11).
limits_future: No implementation; open: when to update the row partition, efficient solvers for cSP and rSP, which pricing problem to call, many incompatible columns or their single convex combination, relaxed compatibility (p. 14); the compatibility constraints of cSP may destroy the pricing structure (p. 6).

method_links.note: Steps 1, 2, 4 (co-authored, third author): starts from the tailing-off effect of degenerate masters (the field's effect, not his own code's), unifies IPS and DCA in one notation and one algorithm, and states as a theorem a result not explicit in the IPS papers

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: turn the complicating feature into an advantage
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: degeneracy, the cause of tailing-off, becomes the source of a smaller working basis and of nondegenerate pivots; also S049 p. 1, S026 p. 10

transferable: When a master LP solution has p < m positive variables, drop the m - p zero rows and price for columns in the span of the positive columns; every such compatible column with negative reduced cost gives a strictly improving pivot (pp. 4-6)

If no single compatible column exists, price a convex combination of incompatible columns whose image on the dropped rows is zero (rSP); its optimal value is a necessary and sufficient optimality certificate (pp. 6, 10)
Before relying on a reformulated pricing problem, prove that it does not depend on an arbitrary choice (here the working basis) with a row-duplication argument (appendix, pp. 15-17)
coauthors: Jacques Desrosiers, Jean Bertrand Gauthier (GERAD & HEC Montréal)

quotes.text: This methodological paper generalizes the improved primal simplex and dynamic constraints aggregation methods.
Combining column generation and dynamic row-partition during the solution process allows for exploiting both the modeling structure of its formulation and the algebraic structure of its solutions.

title: Decomposition theorems for linear programs
contribution: Re-proves the network Flow Decomposition Theorem by a Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation and generalizes it, the Augmenting Cycle Theorem and the Negative Cycle Optimality Theorem to linear programs in terms of weighted paths and weighted cycles of a residual problem, as groundwork for an LP version of minimum mean cycle-canceling and a column generation variant left open.
problem_entry: The decomposition, augmenting-cycle and negative-cycle theorems of network flow theory underlie strongly polynomial cycle-canceling; the paper carries them over to LP (p. 5).
key_idea: A Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation with a cone subproblem whose extreme rays are paths and cycles, plus a count of the variables of a basic solution, proves flow decomposition (pp. 6-7); adding v = b and Ax - v = 0 gives weighted paths and weighted cycles for LP (pp. 7-8); Theorems 2-4 on decomposition, augmenting weighted cycles and optimality on the residual problem (pp. 8-10).
assumptions: LP min cᵀx, Ax = b, l ≤ x ≤ u with m ≤ n and b ≥ 0 without loss of generality (p. 7); network case: capacitated minimum cost flow with balanced supplies (p. 5); no instances.
proof_devices: Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation with Minkowski-Weyl and the size of a basic solution in place of a constructive proof (pp. 6-8)
Residual-problem change of variables x = x0 + (y→ - y←) (p. 9)
Primal-dual pair of pricing LPs: the smallest reduced cost over free π against a weighted cycle under a convexity constraint, equal by duality (pp. 10-11)
Deliberate reuse of network notation; LP extreme rays cannot be scaled to unit cycles, hence 'weighted' paths and cycles (pp. 7-8)
positioning: Extends the network theory of Ahuja, Magnanti and Orlin and the Goldberg-Tarjan MMCC analysis, with S038 as the refined analysis (p. 5).
writing: Short theorem-proof paper; the discussion is a hedged research programme ('remains to be proven', 'deserves an analysis', p. 11); a warning that network notation is reused on purpose (p. 7).
limits_future: Open: an LP version of MMCC whose convergence remains to be proven and whose complexity deserves an analysis, the scaling impact of the convexity constraint being the obstacle (p. 11); a column generation algorithm on MP(x0) (p. 12); only the first keeps degeneracy immunity (p. 12).

method_links.note: Steps 2 and 5 (co-authored, third author): one notation for network and LP results on purpose; the open steps (LP adaptation of MMCC, its convergence and complexity, a column generation variant) published as a programme

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation as a proof and explanation device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Dantzig-Wolfe replaces the constructive proof of flow decomposition and yields the LP theorems; also S038 p. 19, S049 pp. 18-20

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: harvest the pricing problem beyond one column
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: harvesting information from the subproblem called one of the most successful ideas of column generation; also S049 p. 20, S068 pp. 7-8

transferable: To prove a representation theorem in terms of paths, cycles or rays, write a Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation whose subproblem is a cone, drop the null extreme point and count the variables of a basic solution of the master system (pp. 6-8)

State an optimality test as a primal-dual pair of pricing LPs, the dual maximizing the smallest reduced cost over free duals and the primal finding a normalized improving direction; equal optimal values prove the equivalence of primal and dual optimality conditions (pp. 10-11)
coauthors: Jean Bertrand Gauthier, Jacques Desrosiers (GERAD & HEC Montréal)

quotes.text: This paper generalizes these network flow theorems to linear programming.
One of the most successful ideas of column generation is to harvest a lot of information from the subproblem even though some of it might turn out irrelevant

title: A Branch-Price-and-Cut Algorithm for Packing Cuts in Undirected Graphs
contribution: First computational study of cut packing in undirected graphs: a branch-price-and-cut code on SCIP whose extended formulation is the symmetry-free Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation of a compact model, with min-cut pricing, clique cuts carried into the pricing as hyperedges and an edge-clique-cover bound; it solves random graphs up to 80 and benchmark graphs up to 500 vertices and finds γ(G) close to α(G).
problem_entry: Cut packing was known only from duality, complexity and approximation results (p. 1); no experimental results existed, so a first computational study that checks theory against computational experience (p. 2).
key_idea: Extended formulation = Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation of m min-cut copies with the identical subproblems aggregated (p. 3); min-cut pricing by Stoer-Wagner while duals are nonnegative, a binary program otherwise, with greedy disjoint-cut and max-cut heuristics and a column pool (p. 4); branching on y_ij, then Ryan-Foster (pp. 4-5); clique cuts via hyperedges (p. 5); an edge-clique-cover bound (p. 6).
assumptions: Connected undirected graphs (p. 1); about 100 instances: 10th DIMACS challenge graphs, Trick's coloring graphs, random graphs from Rudy, Randgraph and NetworkX 1.7 (seed 1), MUSKETEER-edited twins (p. 6); bipartite and chordal classes because the problem is polynomial there (pp. 7-8).
proof_devices: Branching rules chosen so that pricing stays combinatorial: the x̄_ij = 1 child keeps the duals nonnegative, pair branching is combinatorial only for few pairs (pp. 4-5)
Clique-cut duals moved to hyperedges so that the root pricing is a hypergraph min-cut (p. 5)
LP gap on a clique: n/2 against an optimum of 1 (p. 5)
W[1]-hardness and NP-hardness of pricing with diff constraints deferred to the full version (pp. 1, 5)
experiments: SCIP 3.0.1 with CPLEX 12.4.0.1, Core i7-2600, 3600 s; the compact model solves 2 of 12 random graphs against 8 (basic extended) and 12 (full code), its solver not named; shifted geometric means without the shift; real graphs 5 of 9 solved against 1 of 9 random twins; hidden-optimum benchmarks fail at the root; on/off ablations as performance profiles (pp. 6-10).
positioning: First computational study after a literature of complexity, approximation and duality results only (pp. 1-2).
writing: Results read against theory: the easy classes are easy (p. 8), and the absent factor-2 gap 'comes as a surprise' (p. 10); size limits stated in numbers (p. 10).
limits_future: Limits: 80 vertices on random graphs, 500 on partitioning benchmarks, 5000 edges on coloring graphs (p. 10); combinatorial pricing mattered less than expected (p. 9). Future: better clique edge covers, other min-cut formulations for pricing, dual variable stabilization (p. 11).

method_links.note: Steps 2, 3, 5, 6: the compact model is run and loses (2 of 12 against 12 of 12); a whole cut is the variable because its pricing problem is a min-cut; built on SCIP; branching on original edge variables first
Steps 5-6: easy and hard classes, real graphs next to random and edited twins, per-component ablations in both directions, failures and size limits in the text
A single seed for the random graphs, shifted geometric means without the shift, and the authors' own compact model as the only baseline (no earlier code existed)

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: pricing-compatibility filter for cuts and branching
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: pool candidate from S077: y_ij branching and the hyperedge transfer of clique duals keep the pricing combinatorial, while Ryan-Foster pairs do not scale combinatorially
the polynomial classes are solved faster, and the theoretical factor-2 gap between α(G) and γ(G) is not observed

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: first computational study of a theory-only problem or proposal
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: no experimental results existed for cut packing; also S068 pp. 2, 11

transferable: When identical subproblems repeat (m copies of a cut), derive the extended formulation by Dantzig-Wolfe and aggregate the copies into one pricing problem; the symmetry goes with them (p. 3)
Prefer branching rules whose children keep the pricing duals nonnegative so that a combinatorial pricing algorithm survives; fall back to binary-program pricing only where it cannot (p. 4)
Carry cut duals into the pricing structure: map each clique cut to a hyperedge that carries its dual and solve the pricing as a hypergraph min-cut (p. 5)
Compute a cheap combinatorial bound (an edge clique cover) once and add its inequalities before column generation starts; here switching it off cost the most performance (pp. 6, 9)
For a problem with known easy classes, generate instances of the easy and the hard classes, and pair each real instance with a random and an edited twin of equal size (pp. 7-8)
coauthors: Martin Bergner, Jonas T. Witt (RWTH Aachen)

quotes.text: We are not aware of any experimental results, neither exact nor approximate, for cut packing; thus we provide the first computational study of the problem.
This comes as a surprise as there is a theoretical gap of a factor of 2 that we do not observe in the instances in our experiments.

title: Dantzig-Wolfe Reformulations for the Stable Set Problem
contribution: Earlier, unpublished 2015 version of the stable-set strength paper (S052): Dantzig-Wolfe reformulations of the edge formulation are no stronger than the LP iff the convexified subgraph is bipartite and give the stable set polytope iff it contains all odd holes, proved with new facet-graph lemmas, with computation explicitly deferred.
problem_entry: Beyond the sandwich P_IP ⊆ P_DW ⊆ P_LP and Geoffrion's necessary condition nothing general is known about the strength of Dantzig-Wolfe reformulations (p. 2); the stable set problem is chosen as well understood, relevant to conflict graphs and set packing, and a benchmark for other relaxations (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Convexified constraints = a subgraph G' = (V, E'); weakest iff G' is bipartite (Theorem 1, p. 5); strongest iff G' contains all odd holes, triangles included (Theorems 2-4, pp. 6, 9-10), via the facet-graph Lemmas 2-4 (pp. 7-9).
assumptions: Pure IPs with bounds (p. 1); maximum weight stable set in the edge formulation with weights in Z≥0 (pp. 3-4); triangles count as odd holes (p. 6); polytope identities; no instances.
proof_devices: Half-integral odd-cycle point: outside STAB(G') by the odd cycle inequality (Theorem 1, p. 5), inside DW(G, G') as the average of two alternating stable sets when one hole edge is not convexified (Theorem 2, p. 6)
Five-node counterexample: odd cycles cannot replace odd holes (p. 6)
Andrásfai-style exchange of two maximum weight stable sets plus a shortest path: every critical edge lies in an odd hole (Lemma 2, pp. 7-8)
Induction over a minimal critical edge set (Lemma 3, p. 9) and a deletion order for a spanning critical subgraph (Lemma 4, p. 9)
Facet-by-facet sufficiency (Theorem 3, pp. 9-10)
experiments: none; computational implications out of scope and experiments announced for future work (p. 11)
positioning: Geoffrion 1974 as the only general predecessor; earlier stable-set Dantzig-Wolfe and Lagrangian work limited to specific subgraph classes (pp. 1-3); a weakened answer to a question in Sewell's thesis (p. 10).
writing: Priority claim hedged with 'To the best of our knowledge' in the abstract and on p. 3 (pp. 1, 3); the focus called 'a seminal step' (p. 10).
limits_future: Deciding whether an edge lies in an odd hole is NP-complete, W[1]-complete by hole size; the strongest reformulation's LP is expected to be too hard to solve in practice (p. 11). Future: reformulations between the extremes (all holes up to size k), node covering and linear ordering as believed direct extensions, general IPs as long-term vision (p. 11).

method_links.note: Order, dated: the theory of both extremes is complete in 2015 without computation and experiments are only announced; the enumeration (S058, SEA 2018) came later. Moves the skill's note that the 2018 study starts from a theorem back to 2015
Exit B: proved for one class, extensions to other problems stated as beliefs, the family between the extremes named as the next step
Claim sized in a theory paper: computation declared out of scope, hardness of recognizing odd holes and the expected LP difficulty stated

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: pool candidate from S052/S058: both extremes characterized and the family between them named next; an earlier version of S052, so not an independent paper

transferable: Before characterizing when a reformulation strengthens the bound, prove the never-helps half from a known integrality result applied to the convexified part (here Nemhauser-Trotter: ESTAB = STAB iff bipartite) (pp. 4-5)

To show that leaving a structure unconvexified loses strength, write a fractional point as the average of two integer solutions of the convexified part that violates a valid inequality of the whole problem (pp. 5-6)

quotes.text: Interestingly, this is already all we know about the strength of Dantzig-Wolfe reformulations of integer programs in general.
We will report on experiments in future work.

title: A Branch-Price-and-Cut Algorithm for Multi-Mode Resource Leveling
contribution: Branch-price-and-cut for multi-mode resource leveling with shift calendars whose shift-configuration master is read as a non-trivial Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation of the time-indexed model; with branching and translated precedence cuts on original variables it solves 50-job instances where CPLEX on the time-indexed model solves a quarter as many.
problem_entry: An industrial turnaround-scheduling problem (p. 1); MIP fails on such scheduling because time-indexed LP bounds are weak and start times smear in fractional solutions (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Configurations (sub-schedules of one resource type in one shift) as variables, priced per shift by a time-indexed MIP (pp. 3-4); read as a Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation of the time-indexed model, which guides branching on R_k, S_j, C_j and the translation of precedence cuts (pp. 4-6); edge-finding propagation and list-scheduling heuristics whose schedules enter as columns (pp. 5-6).
assumptions: Multi-mode non-preemptive jobs needing exactly one resource type, renewable resources with shifts, a fixed horizon (pp. 1-2); the one-resource assumption justified by the data planners can supply (p. 1); generated instances N50E70 and N50E100, 50 each, five calendars, after PSPLib, as no public set fits (p. 6).
proof_devices: Branching and cuts on original variables change only the pricing objective, not its constraints (pp. 5-6)
Pricing NP-hard through its resource leveling special case (p. 4)
Exact pseudo-polynomial separation by sorting (τ_best) next to a greedy τ (p. 7)
Cuts separated only after branching or propagation has fixed the resource capacities (pp. 7-8)
experiments: SCIP 2.0.1 plug-ins against CPLEX 12.2 on the time-indexed model, both single thread on the same Core i7-870, 1800 s, 5% noise threshold; root bound on average per calendar 20-65% above the LP bound, against CPLEX's root after cuts 28% better on hard C1 instances but 44% worse in the worst C2 case; solved counts per calendar; node and time means over commonly solved instances with their counts, shifts not stated; pricing 58-99% of the time in the text though Table 3 lists 0.56; root cuts hurt (pp. 6-10).
positioning: Set against the time-indexed tradition (Pritsker et al.) and earlier column generation lower bounds (Brucker and Knust; Drexl and Kimms); claims to be the first approach that 'works on both ends' (pp. 2-3).
writing: The aim is stated as how far one gets when insisting on optimal solutions (p. 9); closes with modelling advice to give single variables more meaning (p. 10).
limits_future: Pricing dominates the running time (p. 9); node gains from cuts do not carry over to time (p. 8); calendars C1-C3 not elaborated (p. 8). Future: constraint programming or heuristic pricing, more inequalities from the scheduling literature (p. 10).

method_links.note: Steps 2, 3, 5, 6: the classical compact model in CPLEX, same machine and threads, as yardstick; a whole shift schedule as variable because the shift pricing problem is small; SCIP plug-ins; branching and cuts on original variables

Workflow B checkpoint (a), marked [inferred] in SKILL.md, practised in 2015: the root bound is compared with CPLEX's root bound after its own cuts, not only with the LP bound; the gain shrinks and turns negative on some instances
Steps 3, 5, 6: identical conditions with a stated noise level, means over commonly solved instances with their counts, losses printed
Self-generated test set, no shift values, C1-C3 profiles left out, and the text's pricing-share range does not cover Table 3

transferable: Decompose a time-indexed scheduling model along its calendar: one pricing problem per resource and shift, each returning whole sub-schedules (pp. 3-5)

Branch first on variables with large objective effect that also restrict the pricing domain (capacities R_k), then on the start or completion time whose fractional configurations lie farthest apart in time (p. 5)

While classical IP modeling used variables with “little meaning” our study supports the advise to impose more structure on a single variable’s meaning.

title: About the minimum mean cycle-canceling algorithm
contribution: A unifying re-presentation of the minimum mean cycle-canceling algorithm through LP duality and a phase-based analysis that, with a new approximation structure in Cancel-and-Tighten, lowers its running time to O(m²n log n) for arbitrary real costs, illustrated on one large network.
problem_entry: Expository entry: centralize Goldberg-Tarjan (1989) and Radzik-Goldberg (1994) in one accessible text with LP arguments in place of constructive ones (abstract, p. 1), claimed to be much more than a synthesis (p. 1).
key_idea: Pricing as a primal-dual LP pair on the residual network (pp. 4-5); the analysis in phases ended by Type 2 cycles (Definition 1, p. 8); Cancel-and-Tighten with level-based potential updates L(b) and L(c) (Proposition 14, p. 15), giving O(mn) phases of O(m log n) time each (Theorem 6, p. 17; Table 1, p. 18).
assumptions: Capacitated minimum cost flow on a directed network with lower and upper bounds and balanced supplies (p. 2); integer costs for Theorem 1 (p. 8), arbitrary real costs for Theorems 2, 3 and 6 (pp. 10, 12, 17).
proof_devices: LP duality and complementary slackness for the pricing step (Proposition 3, p. 7)
A fixed reference potential over a sequence of iterations with Type 1 and Type 2 cycles for the (1 - 1/n) jump (Proposition 5, p. 8)
Geometric progression of the optimality parameter (Theorem 1, p. 8)
Arc fixing (Propositions 8-9, p. 9) and implicit arc fixing with optimal potentials that exist but are unknown (Propositions 10-13, pp. 10-11)
Tighter jump factor by the size of the Type 2 cycle (eq. 16, p. 11)
Exact poll of the optimality parameter every n phases, amortized (Theorem 5, p. 17)
Propositions 6, 7, 9, 11, 14 and Theorem 6 carry no citation; the others are attributed to Goldberg-Tarjan or Radzik-Goldberg (pp. 8-10, 15, 17)
experiments: Illustration only, iterations and phases without times or hardware: a maximum flow network with 502 nodes and 10,007 arcs (p. 5) and one capacitated network of unnamed source with 1025 nodes and 91,220 arcs: 1937 iterations, 87 against 90 phases from two starts, 88 phases with optimal updates, 343 with L(b), 464 with update (d), over 7000 additional phases with L(a) (pp. 13-16).
positioning: Goldberg-Tarjan and Radzik-Goldberg credited result by result; the authors say where they cannot tell their predecessors' intent (pp. 2, 5, 7).
writing: Claims to be much more than a synthesis (p. 1); the conclusion separates four contributions from the review (p. 19).
limits_future: Tailing-off persists in the phase-based version (p. 18); the usefulness of L(c) is still unclear (p. 19); one illustrative instance besides the maximum flow example (pp. 5, 13). Future: generalizations to LP and links to IPS (p. 19).

method_links.note: Steps 2 and 4 (co-authored, third author): a review that puts two papers into one LP notation ends with a new bound and, in the authors' words, became more than a summary; what cannot be established about the sources is said as such
The computational part is one network of unnamed source without times or hardware; practical advice is drawn from it, labelled as an interpretation

Keep node potentials fixed during a phase and cancel cycles only in the admissible subgraph of negative reduced cost arcs, which gets sparser with every cancellation (p. 14)
To keep a complexity bound while estimating the duals, update the estimates so that the jump inequality still holds (eq. 19, p. 15) and poll the exact value only every n phases, amortized (p. 17)
coauthors: Jean Bertrand Gauthier, Jacques Desrosiers (corresponding author) (GERAD & HEC Montréal)

title: Separation of generic cutting planes in branch-and-price using a basis
contribution: First implementation and computational study, in GCG, of Range's basis separation, which applies basis-derived cuts such as GMI cuts for the original problem in branch-price-and-cut through auxiliary vertices of the original LP; with new face-objective heuristics and strengthening inequalities it closes part of the root gap and saves nodes and time where the gap is not too small.
problem_entry: The projection of a basic master solution is generally not basic in the original LP relaxation, so basis-derived cuts are not directly applicable (pp. 1, 3); Range's remedy had no computational study and an unsuccessful preliminary one, known by personal communication (p. 2).
key_idea: Algorithm 1: separate an auxiliary vertex of the original LP near the projected point and keep the cuts that the projected point violates (p. 4); new basis heuristics, a k-extended face objective and α(x̄)-weighted combinations with the original objective (pp. 5-7); strengthening before separation by objective, reduced cost and pricing cuts (pp. 7-8).
assumptions: MIP with Dx ≥ d convexified (p. 2); added inequalities valid because conv(X) ⊇ P_DW (pp. 7-8); test sets capacitated p-median, generalized assignment, temporal knapsack, lot sizing and MIPLIB 2003/2010 instances previously tested with generic branch-price-and-cut, only those where root separation applied (p. 8); instance counts per set not in the text.
proof_devices: Cuts in original variables leave the pricing set unchanged, cuts in master variables do not (p. 3)

Proposition 1 (Range): the projected point is optimal with value zero for the face objective, so a simplex vertex lies in the smallest face containing it and differs from it iff it is not basic (p. 6)
No guarantee that the projected point is cut off (p. 5)
α(x̄) from a QR decomposition with column pivoting (GSL); aggressive SCIP separators, root node only, p_min = 1, i_max = 100 (p. 8)
experiments: GCG 2.0.1 on a development SCIP 3.1.0 with CPLEX 12.5.0.0, Core i7-2600, 3600 s; GCG default against four basis heuristics, the variant picked in preliminary tests; root gap as shifted geometric mean (shift 1), node and time ratios (shifts 100 and 10); 8-ext-conv closes 8%, 33% and 37% of the gap on easy p-median, MIPLIB and lot sizing sets, up to 8% on hard sets; time down by up to 12% (lot sizing) and 30% (MIPLIB), slightly up on generalized assignment and temporal knapsack; strengthening not solely positive (pp. 8-10).
positioning: Such a procedure was mentioned by many authors but presented only by Range; his approach is discussed and extended and his face objective re-implemented as a setting (pp. 2, 5, 8, 11); Dash and Goycoolea's basis heuristics named as a future source (p. 11).
writing: The implementation is called 'the first of its kind' (p. 1); mixed results stated plainly, each strengthening setting giving the smallest gap on some test set (p. 10).
limits_future: No guarantee that the projected point is cut off (p. 5), root node only (p. 8), results on strengthening not clear (p. 11). Future: inequalities with purely positive influence, infeasible-basis heuristics, making the projected point basic for reduced cost fixing, and the relation between reformulation strength and separation success (p. 11).

method_links.note: Step 6: separation in original variables because such cuts leave the pricing problem unchanged; the master solution is projected to the original space before separating

Steps 1, 3, 5: the predecessor's procedure, published without a computational study, implemented as settings in the same code under the same conditions after asking him about his unpublished preliminary study; sets where cuts can show and where they cannot, with the time cost; shifts stated; preliminary tests pick the variant analysed in full
The solved count is said to be slightly increased without a number, and the instance counts per test set are not given

Our experiments suggest that there is a strong relation between the strength of the Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation and the success of separating violated cuts in the original problem.

title: Tools for primal degenerate linear programs: IPS, DCA, and PE
contribution: A survey of three tools against primal degeneracy in LP, the Improved Primal Simplex, Dynamic Constraints Aggregation and the Positive Edge rule, unified in a linear algebra framework of subspace bases in which IPS is a dynamic Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition and DCA a possibly over-spanning basis, with computational results reported from the literature.
problem_entry: Degenerate pivots threaten simplex convergence and hit column generation, above all set partitioning relaxations in routing and crew scheduling (p. 2); a degeneracy level is defined (p. 4); the three tools are described in one framework (pp. 1, 3-4).
key_idea: IPS works on the rows of nondegenerate variables and prices a negative reduced cost convex combination, so every pivot is nondegenerate (pp. 1, 5); compatibility as membership in the subspace V(A_F) (pp. 15-16); a larger subspace basis covers DCA (pp. 17-18, 28-29); IPS as a dynamic Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition (pp. 18-20); PE as a stochastic membership test (pp. 34-35).
assumptions: LP with bounded variables, m < n, A of full row rank, feasible and bounded (p. 5); DCA for set partitioning only (p. 29); no data of its own.
proof_devices: Proposition 1: the IPS optimality condition, by dual feasibility one way and a strictly improving combination the other (p. 11)
Propositions 2-3: independence from the row partition and the span characterization of compatibility (pp. 15-16)
Rough estimate 1 - (1/2)^(r-f) of the chance of a degenerate pivot with an over-spanning subspace basis (p. 17)
Implementation devices: compatible restricted master, multiple improving directions, surrogate variables split into components, three partial pricing biases (pp. 19-24)
experiments: No own runs; results reported from the literature: IPS 3.53 times faster than CPLEX's primal simplex on 10 vehicle and crew scheduling LPs and 12.30 times (20.23 with upper bounds) on 14 fleet assignment LPs (p. 25); DCA variants in GENCOL by 'factors of 50 to 100', compounded as in the listed papers (p. 33); PE neutral below 25% degeneracy and 2.72 times faster above it on 32 LPs from Mittelmann's library (p. 35).
positioning: IPS as the starting point that explains DCA, 'an intuitive precursor to IPS' (p. 28), and PE (pp. 3-4); 'the first time DCA and IPS are studied in parallel' (p. 28).
writing: A survey with its own unifying terminology (p. 5); plain warnings against the literature's equation of compatibility with nondegenerate pivots (pp. 17-18).
limits_future: A general implementation is a major concern and the improved pricing step is the bottleneck (p. 36). Future: automating the trigger points of the acceleration ideas, column generation, dual simplex, convex optimization, sensitivity analysis under degeneracy, an integral simplex for set partitioning (pp. 36-37).
